claim: Escherichia coli uses a single chemotaxis protein network to navigate gradients of chemical attractants and repellents, as well as gradients of temperature, oxygen, and pH.
source: Escherichia coli uses a single chemotaxis protein network to navigate gradients of chemical attractants and repellents, as well as gradients of temperature, oxygen, and pH (Sourjik and Wingreen, 2012) (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sourjik and Wingreen, 2012

claim: The core of the E. coli chemotaxis network is a two-component signal transduction system that carries chemical information from transmembrane receptors to flagellar motors.
source: The core of the network is a two-component signal transduction system that carries chemical information gathered by transmembrane receptors to flagellar motors responsible for cell propulsion.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge about E. coli chemotaxis network architecture

claim: A second group of proteins in the chemotaxis network allows cells to physiologically adapt to changing background signal levels.
source: A second group of proteins allows the cells to physiologically adapt to changing background signal levels, enabling them to track signal gradients over many orders of magnitude.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge about chemotaxis adaptation

claim: The chemotaxis adaptation system enables cells to track signal gradients over many orders of magnitude.
source: A second group of proteins allows the cells to physiologically adapt to changing background signal levels, enabling them to track signal gradients over many orders of magnitude.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge about the functional capability of the adaptation system

claim: All signals in E. coli chemotaxis are processed through the same set of cytoplasmic proteins responsible for signal transduction and adaptation.
source: While different receptors allow cells to sense different signals, all signals are then processed through the same set of cytoplasmic proteins responsible for signal transduction and adaptation.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge about the architecture of the chemotaxis network

claim: E. coli explores its environment by alternating between straight runs and direction-changing tumbles.
source: The cell uses flagella to explore its environment in a run-and-tumble fashion (Berg and Brown, 1972).
evidence: Supported by citation to Berg and Brown, 1972

claim: Counterclockwise rotation of flagella promotes the formation of a helical bundle that propels the cell forward in a run.
source: Counterclockwise rotation of the flagella promotes the formation of a helical bundle that propels the cell forward in a run.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge about flagellar motor function

claim: Clockwise rotation of flagella tends to disrupt the bundle, interrupting runs with brief direction-changing tumbles.
source: Clockwise rotation tends to disrupt the bundle, interrupting runs with brief direction-changing tumbles.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge about flagellar motor function

claim: Clockwise bias controls the frequency of tumbles and plays a central role in chemotactic behavior.
source: The fraction of time a motor spins clockwise, or clockwise bias, controls the frequency of tumbles and thus plays a central role in chemotactic behavior.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge about the relationship between clockwise bias and tumbling

claim: Tumble frequency increases monotonically with clockwise bias until the latter reaches about 0.9.
source: Tumble frequency increases monotonically with clockwise bias until the latter reaches about 0.9, at which point cells tumble nearly twice a second and are essentially stationary (Alon et al., 1998).
evidence: Supported by citation to Alon et al., 1998

claim: At clockwise bias of about 0.9, cells tumble nearly twice a second and are essentially stationary.
source: Tumble frequency increases monotonically with clockwise bias until the latter reaches about 0.9, at which point cells tumble nearly twice a second and are essentially stationary (Alon et al., 1998).
evidence: Supported by citation to Alon et al., 1998

claim: Clonal cells grown and observed under the same conditions without stimulation differ substantially in clockwise bias.
source: It has been observed that clonal cells, grown and observed under the same conditions without stimulation, will differ substantially in clockwise bias (Park et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Park et al., 2010

claim: The central logic of E. coli chemotaxis is to transiently decrease clockwise bias in response to an increase in attractant signal.
source: The central logic of E. coli chemotaxis is to transiently decrease clockwise bias in response to an increase in attractant signal (Figure 1B).
evidence: Stated as established knowledge and illustrated in Figure 1B

claim: Cells climb gradients of attractants by lengthening runs up the gradient.
source: This approach allows cells to climb gradients of attractants by lengthening runs up the gradient (Figure 1C).
evidence: Stated as established knowledge and illustrated in Figure 1C

claim: The adaptation process that maintains receptor sensitivity is mediated by covalent modification of chemoreceptors through addition and subtraction of methyl groups by CheR and CheB.
source: The adaptation process that maintains receptor sensitivity is mediated by the covalent modification of the chemoreceptors through addition and subtraction of methyl groups by the enzymes CheR and CheB, respectively.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge about the molecular mechanism of adaptation

claim: The timescale of the adaptation process varies among clonal cells.
source: Like clockwise bias, the timescale of this adaptation process has been observed to vary among clonal cells (Spudich and Koshland, 1976).
evidence: Supported by citation to Spudich and Koshland, 1976

claim: The intracellular levels of CheR and CheB change both adaptation timescale and clockwise bias.
source: The intracellular levels of these proteins are known to change both adaptation timescale and clockwise bias (Alon et al., 1999).
evidence: Supported by citation to Alon et al., 1999

claim: Chemoreceptor activity is communicated to the motors via phosphorylation of CheY to form CheY-P by the receptor-associated kinase CheA.
source: Chemoreceptor activity is communicated to the motors via phosphorylation of the response regulator CheY to form CheY-P by the receptor-associated kinase CheA.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge about signal transduction mechanism

claim: CheZ opposes the action of CheA by dephosphorylating CheY-P.
source: CheZ opposes the action of CheA by dephosphorylating CheY-P.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge about CheZ function

claim: The balance of CheA and CheZ affects clockwise bias.
source: Consequently, the balance of CheA and CheZ affects clockwise bias.
evidence: Logical inference from the opposing actions of CheA and CheZ on CheY-P levels

claim: The total amount of CheY in the cell determines the range of possible CheY-P levels.
source: The total amount of CheY in the cell determines the range of possible CheY-P levels, and due to noise in the expression of CheY (Kollmann et al., 2005) this dynamic range will likewise vary between clonal cells.
evidence: Logical inference supported by citation to Kollmann et al., 2005 regarding noise in CheY expression

claim: Due to noise in the expression of CheY, the dynamic range of CheY-P varies between clonal cells.
source: The total amount of CheY in the cell determines the range of possible CheY-P levels, and due to noise in the expression of CheY (Kollmann et al., 2005) this dynamic range will likewise vary between clonal cells.
evidence: Supported by citation to Kollmann et al., 2005

claim: Clockwise bias, adaptation time, and CheY-P dynamic range are the main determinants of how E. coli performs chemotaxis.
source: These three phenotypic parameters—clockwise bias, adaptation time, and CheY-P dynamic range—are the main determinants of how E. coli performs chemotaxis.
evidence: Stated as a conclusion from the preceding discussion of these parameters

claim: The phenotypic parameters depend on the quantities of chemotaxis proteins within each individual cell.
source: These in turn depend on the quantities of chemotaxis proteins within each individual cell.
evidence: Logical inference from the relationships described between protein levels and phenotypic parameters

claim: The copy numbers of chemotaxis proteins directly determine the ability of the individual to navigate its environment.
source: Hence, the copy numbers of these proteins directly determine the ability of the individual to navigate its environment.
evidence: Logical inference from the relationship between protein levels, phenotypic parameters, and chemotactic performance

claim: The dependency of chemotactic performance on protein levels is independent of the type of signal being followed.
source: Since all signals are processed through the same core proteins, this dependency should be independent of the type of signal being followed.
evidence: Logical inference from the fact that all signals are processed through the same proteins

claim: Cell-to-cell variability in protein abundance is likely a major contributor to observed non-genetic behavioral diversity in clonal populations.
source: As such, cell-to-cell variability in protein abundance is likely a major contributor to the observed non-genetic behavioral diversity in clonal populations (Figure 1D, First and second panels).
evidence: Inference from the relationships established between protein levels and behavior, illustrated in Figure 1D

claim: Noise in gene expression contributes to variability in protein abundance.
source: Various mechanisms can contribute to such variability, including noise in gene expression (Elowitz et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citation to Elowitz et al., 2002

claim: Random segregation of proteins during cell division probably plays a role in protein abundance variability.
source: Random segregation of proteins during cell division probably plays a role as well (Huh and Paulsson, 2011) and may impose a lower bound on minimum variability attainable (Lestas et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to Huh and Paulsson, 2011 and Lestas et al., 2010

claim: Random segregation of proteins during cell division may impose a lower bound on minimum variability attainable.
source: Random segregation of proteins during cell division probably plays a role as well (Huh and Paulsson, 2011) and may impose a lower bound on minimum variability attainable (Lestas et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lestas et al., 2010

claim: Chemotaxis genes are chromosomally organized in operons.
source: Chemotaxis genes are chromosomally organized in operons—that is, expression of multiple genes are driven by common promoters.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge about E. coli chemotaxis gene organization

claim: Operon organization ensures that noise in the activity of shared promoters affects the expression of multiple genes in a correlated manner.
source: This genetic architecture ensures that noise in the activity of shared promoters will affect the expression of multiple genes in a correlated manner, conserving the ratios of proteins from cell to cell despite variations in total amounts (Lovdok et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lovdok et al., 2009

claim: Operon organization conserves the ratios of proteins from cell to cell despite variations in total amounts.
source: This genetic architecture ensures that noise in the activity of shared promoters will affect the expression of multiple genes in a correlated manner, conserving the ratios of proteins from cell to cell despite variations in total amounts (Lovdok et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lovdok et al., 2009

claim: Correlation in protein noise has been experimentally shown to be important in determining chemotactic performance.
source: Correlation in protein noise has been experimentally shown to be important in determining chemotactic performance (Lovdok et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lovdok et al., 2007

claim: Conservation of protein ratios greatly reduces the occurrence of cells with unacceptable parameter values.
source: Combined with the negative integral feedback design of the protein network, this conservation of protein ratios greatly reduces the occurrence of cells with unacceptable parameter values—for instance, those that only run or only tumble—and maintains the precision of the physiological adaptation process (Alon et al., 1999; Kollmann et al., 2005; Barkai and Leibler, 1997; Yi et al., 2000).
evidence: Supported by citations to Alon et al., 1999; Kollmann et al., 2005; Barkai and Leibler, 1997; Yi et al., 2000

claim: Conservation of protein ratios maintains the precision of the physiological adaptation process.
source: Combined with the negative integral feedback design of the protein network, this conservation of protein ratios greatly reduces the occurrence of cells with unacceptable parameter values—for instance, those that only run or only tumble—and maintains the precision of the physiological adaptation process (Alon et al., 1999; Kollmann et al., 2005; Barkai and Leibler, 1997; Yi et al., 2000).
evidence: Supported by citations to Alon et al., 1999; Kollmann et al., 2005; Barkai and Leibler, 1997; Yi et al., 2000

claim: Chemotaxis in E. coli is often said to be robust.
source: For these and other reasons (Oleksiuk et al., 2011; Endres and Wingreen, 2006; Sneddon et al., 2012; Vladimirov et al., 2010; Schulmeister etl., 2011), chemotaxis in E. coli is often said to be robust.
evidence: Supported by citations to Oleksiuk et al., 2011; Endres and Wingreen, 2006; Sneddon et al., 2012; Vladimirov et al., 2010; Schulmeister et al., 2011

claim: Within the range of acceptable behaviors, substantial variability exists in chemotactic behavior.
source: Within this range of acceptable behaviors, however, substantial variability exists, and the fact that this variability has not been selected against raises the question of whether it might serve an adaptive function.
evidence: Stated as an observation that motivates the research question

claim: Population diversity is known to be an adaptive strategy for environmental uncertainty.
source: Population diversity is known to be an adaptive strategy for environmental uncertainty (Donaldson-Matasci et al., 2008; Kussell and Leibler, 2005; Haccou and Iwasa, 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to Donaldson-Matasci et al., 2008; Kussell and Leibler, 2005; Haccou and Iwasa, 2005

claim: Past simulations have shown that the speed at which cells climb exponential gradients depends on clockwise bias and adaptation time.
source: Indeed, past simulations (Vladimirov et al., 2008; Jiang et al., 2010; Dufour et al., 2014) have shown that the speed at which cells climb exponential gradients depends on clockwise bias and adaptation time, and experiments (Park et al., 2011) using the capillary assay—an experiment that tests cells' ability to find the mouth of a pipette filled with attractant—have shown that inducing expression of CheR and CheB at different levels changes the chemotactic response.
evidence: Supported by citations to Vladimirov et al., 2008; Jiang et al., 2010; Dufour et al., 2014

claim: Experiments using the capillary assay have shown that inducing expression of CheR and CheB at different levels changes the chemotactic response.
source: Indeed, past simulations (Vladimirov et al., 2008; Jiang et al., 2010; Dufour et al., 2014) have shown that the speed at which cells climb exponential gradients depends on clockwise bias and adaptation time, and experiments (Park et al., 2011) using the capillary assay—an experiment that tests cells' ability to find the mouth of a pipette filled with attractant—have shown that inducing expression of CheR and CheB at different levels changes the chemotactic response.
evidence: Supported by citation to Park et al., 2011

claim: E. coli and other freely swimming bacteria encounter a wide variety of environments.
source: Relatively little is known about the ecology of E. coli chemotaxis, but it is probable that they, like other freely swimming bacteria, encounter a wide variety of environments, from gradients whipped up by turbulent eddies (Taylor and Stocker, 2012) to those generated during the consumption of large nutrient caches (Blackburn et al., 1998; Saragosti et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Taylor and Stocker, 2012; Blackburn et al., 1998; Saragosti et al., 2011

claim: Variations in environmental parameters change the steepness of gradients over orders of magnitude.
source: In each case, variations in environmental parameters, such as in the amount of turbulence, the diffusivity of the nutrients, or the number of cells, will change the steepness of these gradients over orders of magnitude (Taylor and Stocker, 2012; Stocker at al., 2008; Seymour et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to Taylor and Stocker, 2012; Stocker et al., 2008; Seymour et al., 2009

claim: Chemotactic performance depends on how the phenotype of the individual matches the length- and time-scales of the environment.
source: Chemotactic performance, or the ability of cells to achieve a spatial advantage over time, will depend on how the phenotype of the individual matches the length- and time-scales of the environment.
evidence: Stated as a hypothesis based on the relationship between phenotype and environmental parameters

claim: It would seem unlikely that a single phenotype would optimally prepare a population for all environments.
source: Considering the variety of scales in the aforementioned challenges, and the fact that all must be processed by the same proteins (Figure 1A), it would seem unlikely that a single phenotype would optimally prepare a population for all environments, potentially leading to performance trade-offs (Figure 1D, panel 3) wherein mutual optimization of multiple tasks with a single phenotype is not possible.
evidence: Logical inference from the variety of environmental scales and the constraint of using the same proteins

claim: Selection that acts on chemotactic performance could transform performance trade-offs into fitness trade-offs.
source: Therefore, selection that acts on chemotactic performance could transform performance trade-offs into fitness trade-offs (Figure 1D, panels 3 and 4), which are known to have direct consequences for the evolution of diversity (Donaldson and Matasci et al., 2008; Kussell and Leibler, 2005; Haccou and Iwasa, 1995; Shoval et al., 2012).
evidence: Logical inference supported by citations to Donaldson-Matasci et al., 2008; Kussell and Leibler, 2005; Haccou and Iwasa, 1995; Shoval et al., 2012

claim: Fitness trade-offs are known to have direct consequences for the evolution of diversity.
source: Therefore, selection that acts on chemotactic performance could transform performance trade-offs into fitness trade-offs (Figure 1D, panels 3 and 4), which are known to have direct consequences for the evolution of diversity (Donaldson and Matasci et al., 2008; Kussell and Leibler, 2005; Haccou and Iwasa, 1995; Shoval et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Donaldson-Matasci et al., 2008; Kussell and Leibler, 2005; Haccou and Iwasa, 1995; Shoval et al., 2012

claim: Selection that favors top performers disproportionately to intermediate performers could transform a weak performance trade-off into a strong fitness trade-off.
source: Selection that favors top performers disproportionately to intermediate performers could hypothetically transform a weak performance trade-off into a strong fitness trade-off.
evidence: Stated as a hypothesis about the effect of selection on trade-offs

claim: Fitness trade-offs can lead to the development of multiple biological modules.
source: Fitness trade-offs can lead to the development of multiple biological modules (Reuffler et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Reuffler et al., 2012

claim: Bet-hedging is a strategy used by bacteria to avoid extinction from antibiotic stress during infection.
source: This latter case, often called 'bet-hedging (Veening et al., 2008),' is a strategy used by bacteria to avoid extinction from antibiotic stress during infection (Stewart and Cookson, 2012) and has evolved in the laboratory under fluctuating selection (Beaumount et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to Veening et al., 2008; Stewart and Cookson, 2012; Beaumont et al., 2009

claim: Bet-hedging has evolved in the laboratory under fluctuating selection.
source: This latter case, often called 'bet-hedging (Veening et al., 2008),' is a strategy used by bacteria to avoid extinction from antibiotic stress during infection (Stewart and Cookson, 2012) and has evolved in the laboratory under fluctuating selection (Beaumount et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Beaumont et al., 2009

claim: The model simultaneously fit the mean behavior of the population and the noisy distribution of single-cell behaviors.
source: By combining these components, our model simultaneously fit the mean behavior of the population (Kollmann et al., 2005) and the noisy distribution of single-cell behaviors (Park et al., 2010) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kollmann et al., 2005 and Park et al., 2010, and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1

claim: In the model, the only driver of behavioral differences between cells is differences in protein abundance.
source: In all cases, a single set of fixed biochemical parameters was used, the only driver of behavioral differences between cells being differences in protein abundance.
evidence: Stated as a feature of the model design

claim: When a nearby source appeared in the foraging challenge, successful cells had high clockwise bias and short adaptation time.
source: When a nearby source appeared, cells in the foraging challenge immediately experienced high nutrient levels and were challenged to maintain their position despite having been exposed to a large increase in signal. Successful cells had high clockwise bias, which curtails long runs, and short adaptation time, which mitigates large responses (Figure 2B).
evidence: Shown in simulation results in Figure 2B

claim: When a source appeared farther away in the foraging challenge, cells had to use longer runs to reach the expanding front of the gradient and long adaptation times to integrate the weaker signals at its tails.
source: Conversely, when a source appeared farther away, cells had to use longer runs to reach the expanding front of the gradient and long adaptation times to integrate the weaker signals at its tails (Figure 2C).
evidence: Shown in simulation results in Figure 2C

claim: In the colonization case, shorter adaptation times were favored overall as compared to foraging.
source: The case of colonization was similar, except that shorter adaptation times were favored overall as compared to foraging.
evidence: Shown in simulation results comparing colonization and foraging

claim: The gradient geometry is much steeper in the vicinity of the colonization source due to its persistently high concentration.
source: This was because the gradient geometry is much steeper in the vicinity of the source due to its persistently high concentration, and climbing that final part of the gradient was required for colonization (Figure 2D inset vs. A inset).
evidence: Shown in Figure 2D inset vs. A inset

claim: Climbing steep gradients requires fast adaptation to stay abreast of quickly changing background levels.
source: Climbing steep gradients requires fast adaptation to stay abreast of quickly changing background levels.
evidence: Logical inference from the relationship between gradient steepness and adaptation requirements

claim: The source concentration played a minor role in colonization.
source: The source concentration played a minor role in colonization; however, when foraging less concentrated sources, the favored strategy for far distances inverts from low to high clockwise bias, indicating that at that point little can be gained from motility—in fact higher motility may move the cell away from the source (Figure 2—figure supplement 7).
evidence: Shown in simulation results in Figure 2—figure supplement 7

claim: The dynamic range of CheY-P has a negligible effect on cell performance so long as it is sufficiently high.
source: The dynamic range of CheY-P has a negligible effect on cell performance so long as it is sufficiently high as to ensure that the response of CheY-P to kinase activity is linear and does not saturate (Figure 2—figure supplement 8).
evidence: Shown in simulation results in Figure 2—figure supplement 8

claim: In both foraging and colonization challenges, the distance at which the source appeared substantially changed which phenotypes outperformed the others.
source: In both challenges, the distance at which the source appeared substantially changed which phenotypes outperformed the others.
evidence: Shown in simulation results comparing different source distances

claim: Distant sources required lower clockwise bias and longer adaptation time than nearby ones.
source: In general, distant sources required lower clockwise bias and longer adaptation time than nearby ones (Figure 2C compared to B and F compared to E).
evidence: Shown in simulation results in Figures 2B, C, E, F

claim: The dependence of the optimal phenotype on the environment follows the same trend in the previous analytical model as it does in the current simulation results.
source: The dependence of the optimal phenotype on the environment follows the same trend in the previous analytical model as it does in our current simulation results, wherein simulations of distant sources are similar to simple shallow gradients and nearer sources are analogous to steeper gradients.
evidence: Comparison with previous analytical model results from Dufour et al., 2014

claim: Trade-offs in performance arose when cells were required to mutually optimize foraging or colonization of nearby and far away sources.
source: Trade-offs in performance arose when cells were required to mutually optimize foraging or colonization of nearby and far away sources (Figure 4).
evidence: Shown in simulation results in Figure 4

claim: As the disparity between source distances becomes greater, the front of the trade-off transitions from convex to concave.
source: As the disparity between these source distances becomes greater, the front of the trade-off transitions from convex to concave (Figure 4, from A–C for foraging and from D–F for colonization), demonstrating that performance trade-offs in fundamental tasks can be strong when environmental variability is high.
evidence: Shown in simulation results in Figure 4

claim: Performance trade-offs in fundamental tasks can be strong when environmental variability is high.
source: As the disparity between these source distances becomes greater, the front of the trade-off transitions from convex to concave (Figure 4, from A–C for foraging and from D–F for colonization), demonstrating that performance trade-offs in fundamental tasks can be strong when environmental variability is high.
evidence: Shown in simulation results in Figure 4

claim: Trade-offs become much stronger when the environment turns over rapidly.
source: Trade-offs become much stronger when the environment turns over rapidly (Figure 2—figure supplement 6).
evidence: Shown in simulation results in Figure 2—figure supplement 6

claim: When the nutrition requirement was low and the dependency was weak, the previously neutral trade-off became a weak fitness trade-off.
source: When the nutrition requirement was low and the dependency was weak, the previously neutral trade-off became a weak fitness trade-off (Figure 5B).
evidence: Shown in simulation results in Figure 5B

claim: Increasing the nutrition requirement and dependency imposed stricter selection, which penalized all but the top performers and transformed the underlying neutral performance trade-off into a strong fitness trade-off.
source: Increasing the nutrition requirement and dependency imposed stricter selection, which penalized all but the top performers. This transformed the underlying neutral performance trade-off into a strong fitness trade-off (Figure 5C).
evidence: Shown in simulation results in Figure 5C

claim: The selection parameters themselves can determine the strength of fitness trade-offs.
source: Therefore, the selection parameters themselves can determine the strength of fitness trade-offs.
evidence: Conclusion from the simulation results showing how selection parameters affect trade-off strength

claim: When the time limit for colonization was high, the previously neutral performance trade-off gave rise to a weak fitness trade-off.
source: When the time limit was high, the previously neutral performance trade-off gave rise to a weak fitness trade-off (Figure 5E).
evidence: Shown in simulation results in Figure 5E

claim: When the time limit for colonization was lower, the same performance trade-off became a strong fitness trade-off.
source: When the transition point was lower, the same performance trade-off became a strong fitness trade-off (Figure 5F).
evidence: Shown in simulation results in Figure 5F

claim: The nonlinear relationship between performance and fitness can increase or reduce the fitness difference between high-performing specialists and intermediate-performing generalist.
source: The common thread between these cases is that the nonlinear relationship between performance and fitness can increase or reduce the fitness difference between the high-performing specialists and intermediate-performing generalist, strengthening or weakening the trade-off, respectively.
evidence: Conclusion from the simulation results showing how nonlinear selection affects trade-offs

claim: Whether diversification is advantageous depends not only on performance trade-offs, but also on the selection process.
source: Thus, whether diversification is advantageous depends not only on performance trade-offs, but also on the selection process, which has the potential to reverse the strength of trade-offs.
evidence: Conclusion from the simulation results showing the interaction between performance and selection

claim: The model of bacterial chemotaxis, when combined with a model of cell-to-cell variability in protein abundance, reproduces the variability in adaptation time and clockwise bias measured in a wildtype population.
source: As mentioned earlier, our model of bacterial chemotaxis, when combined with a model of cell-to-cell variability in protein abundance, reproduces the variability in adaptation time and clockwise bias measured in a wildtype population (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Shown in model fit to experimental data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1

claim: The fit of the model suggests that noise in protein levels is a plausible driver for behavioral diversity in E. coli chemotaxis.
source: While there are certainly variations in other quantities, such as cell size or number of flagella, the fit of our model suggests that noise in protein levels is a plausible driver for behavioral diversity in E. coli chemotaxis.
evidence: Inference from the model's ability to reproduce experimental data

claim: When populations were optimized for weak trade-off in either foraging or colonization tasks, the resulting populations exhibited lower levels of protein noise in comparison to populations optimized for the respective strong trade-offs.
source: When we optimized populations for weak trade-off in either foraging or colonization tasks, the resulting populations in both tasks exhibited lower levels of protein noise (Figure 7A for foraging and Figure 7E for colonization, blue points) and lower phenotypic variability (Figure 7B,F), in comparison to populations optimized for the respective strong foraging or colonization trade-offs (Figure 7A,B,E,F, red compared to blue points).
evidence: Shown in optimization results in Figure 7

claim: In all optimization cases, the spread of individuals in the optimal populations was constrained to the Pareto front.
source: In all cases, the spread of individuals in the optimal populations was constrained to the Pareto front (Figure 7C,D,G,H).
evidence: Shown in optimization results in Figure 7

claim: The spread of individuals was more condensed in the weak trade-offs than in the strong trade-off in the same task.
source: The spread was more condensed in the weak trade-offs than in the strong trade-off in the same task (Figure 7C compared to D for foraging and G compared to H for colonization).
evidence: Shown in optimization results in Figure 7

claim: In the weak trade-off cases, condensation into a single point on the Pareto front was impeded by lower bounds on noise.
source: In the weak trade-off cases, condensation into a single point on the Pareto front was impeded by lower bounds on noise.
evidence: Conclusion from the optimization results

claim: Adjustments in the means and correlations between protein abundance enabled the system to shape the 'residual' noise to distribute cells along the Pareto front.
source: Even though a pure generalist strategy was unattainable, adjustments in the means and correlations between protein abundance enabled the system to shape the 'residual' noise to distribute cells along the Pareto front.
evidence: Conclusion from the optimization results

claim: Given that molecular noise is irreducible, the best solution may be to constrain diversity to the Pareto front.
source: This could be a general phenomenon in biological systems: given that molecular noise is irreducible, the best solution is to constrain diversity to the Pareto front.
evidence: Speculation based on the optimization results

claim: Mutations in the regulatory elements of a pathway may enable populations to constrain diversity to the Pareto front.
source: Our results suggest this may be achievable via mutations in the regulatory elements of a pathway.
evidence: Speculation based on the optimization results

claim: In the strong foraging trade-off, the optimized population took advantage of the fact that correlated noise in protein levels leads to an inverse relationship between clockwise bias and adaptation time.
source: In the strong foraging trade-off, the optimized population took advantage of the fact that correlated noise in protein levels leads to an inverse relationship between clockwise bias and adaptation time (Figure 7A,B, red) due to the architecture of the network.
evidence: Shown in optimization results in Figure 7A,B

claim: The optimized population for strong foraging trade-off contained specialists for near sources with higher clockwise bias and shorter adaptation times, and specialists for far sources with lower clockwise bias and longer adaptation time.
source: By capitalizing on this feature, the population contained specialists for near sources, which had higher clockwise bias and shorter adaptation times, and those for far sources, which had lower clockwise bias and longer adaptation time.
evidence: Shown in optimization results

claim: In order to achieve greater diversity in clockwise bias while keeping adaptation time low for the strong colonization trade-off, the optimized population had increased intrinsic noise.
source: In order to achieve greater diversity in clockwise bias while keeping adaptation time low, the optimized population for this trade-off had increased intrinsic noise, which diversified protein ratios and disrupted the inverse correlation between clockwise bias and adaptation time (Figure 7E,F, red).
evidence: Shown in optimization results in Figure 7E,F

claim: In all optimization cases, selection on regulatory elements of the network resulted in phenotypic diversity being remarkably constrained to the Pareto front.
source: In all cases, selection on regulatory elements of the network resulted in phenotypic diversity being remarkably constrained to the Pareto front.
evidence: Conclusion from the optimization results

claim: The levels of diversity in the optimized populations are consistent with the sign of the curvature of the Pareto front they occupy.
source: Furthermore, the levels of diversity in these populations are consistent with the sign of the curvature of the Pareto front they occupy.
evidence: Conclusion from the optimization results

claim: Genetic alterations to basic regulatory mechanisms may allow clonal cells to resolve multi-objective problems at the population level using a single signaling network.
source: The adaptability of these distributions predicts that genetic alterations to basic regulatory mechanisms may allow clonal cells to resolve multi-objective problems at the population level using a single signaling network.
evidence: Prediction based on the optimization results

claim: Seeding the same clonal population in different assays that have different length- or time-scales should select for different optimal subpopulations with different phenotypic parameters and different levels of protein expression.
source: First, seeding the same clonal population in different assays that have different length- or time-scales should select for different optimal subpopulations with different phenotypic parameters and different levels of protein expression.
evidence: Prediction based on the simulation results

claim: Experimental work using the capillary assay already supports the claim that different assays select for different subpopulations.
source: Such measurements would make it experimentally possible to verify the chemotactic trade-offs we predict. Experimental work using the capillary assay already supports this claim (Park et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Park et al., 2011

claim: In laboratory evolution with one selection condition, populations will reduce phenotypic diversity but run into a lower limit of protein noise.
source: In the case of laboratory evolution with one selection condition, we predict an eventual shift toward genotypes that suppress population noise, as well as toward mutations in chemotaxis protein RBSs that allow the mean clockwise bias and adaptation time to specialize for this task. In this case, we predict that populations will reduce phenotypic diversity but run into a lower limit of protein noise.

source: A new feature of our conceptual framework is the distinction between performance and fitness. Organisms exhibit many behaviors that, to researchers, are not directly connected to survival and reproduction. These gaps in our understanding inhibit our ability to understand the evolutionary significance of many organismal behaviors. Here, we demonstrated methods for broaching these questions quantitatively, and in so doing uncovered the relevant finding that nonlinearities in selection can strengthen or weaken trade-offs.
evidence: Conclusion from the study results

source: Although the concept of non-genetic individuality may have been initially coined in reference to E. coli chemotaxis (Spudich and Koshland, 1976), we now know that many other biological systems exhibit substantial non-genetic cell-to-cell variability, including stem cell differentiation (Huang, 2009), bacterial sporulation (Maamar.et al., 2007), and cancer cell response to chemotherapy (Spencer et al., 2009).
